## Install pigauto

Install the package before running the examples. The optional torch runtime is
needed only if you plan to fit the graph neural network with `gnn = TRUE`.

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("pigauto")
packageVersion("pigauto")
```

If CRAN has an earlier version than the one described here, install the GitHub
version instead:

```{r install-github, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("pak") # only needed once
pak::pak("itchyshin/pigauto")
```

Install torch only if you plan to use `gnn = TRUE`:

```{r install-torch, eval=FALSE}
torch::install_torch()
```

## Start here

These examples use functions and defaults from pigauto 0.11.0. Check
`packageVersion("pigauto")`: if CRAN has an earlier version, use the GitHub
installation above before following this workflow.
See [the installation steps](#install-pigauto) if you have not installed the
package yet.

Start with the bundled bird data so you can try the workflow before preparing
your own files. The example below hides one measured body-mass value, checks
the inputs, runs the baseline without the optional GNN, and compares the
completed value with the measurement you held back.

This is a mechanics check, not an accuracy assessment: one held-back value is
too little to measure predictive accuracy. For an accuracy assessment, hide a
prespecified set of measured values and compare predictions with all of their
saved measurements. The [validation article](validation-results.html) explains
the package's current evidence and its limits.

```{r first-run, eval=FALSE}
library(pigauto)
data(avonet300, tree300)

traits <- avonet300
rownames(traits) <- traits$Species_Key
traits$Species_Key <- NULL
target <- which(!is.na(traits$Mass))[1L]
truth <- traits$Mass[target]
traits$Mass[target] <- NA_real_

check <- check_pigauto(traits, tree300)
print(check)
if (!check$ready) stop("Fix the input problems reported by check_pigauto().")
result <- impute(traits, tree300, gnn = FALSE)
completed <- completed_data(result)
data.frame(
  species = rownames(traits)[target],
  measured_mass = truth,
  imputed_mass = completed$Mass[target]
)
```

To use your own files instead, prepare a CSV with one row per species and a
unique column that identifies each species. Species names must use the same
spelling as the tree's tip labels, but the two sets do not have to be identical.
Rows for species present only in your data remain in `completed` unchanged;
they are not modeled or filled. Tree tips without a data row can still inform
the fit. This example expects one tree: `read_tree()` returns a
`multiPhylo` collection when the file contains several trees, and
`impute()` requires one `phylo` tree. For a posterior tree sample, use `multi_impute_trees()` in the
experimental [tree-sensitivity workflow](tree-uncertainty.html); its outputs
are prediction diagnostics and have not been validated for downstream
inference. Then replace the bundled objects above with:

```{r file-input-route, eval=FALSE}
traits <- read_traits("traits.csv", species_col = "species")
tree <- read_tree("tree.nwk")
check <- check_pigauto(traits, tree)
print(check)
if (identical(check$status, "not_needed")) {
  message("All matched target cells are observed; no imputation is needed.")
} else if (identical(check$status, "error")) {
  stop("Fix the input problems reported by check_pigauto().")
}
```

If the status is `not_needed`, stop here: there are no missing matched cells to
fill. For `error`, fix the reported input problems and run the check again. If
the status is `ready_with_warnings`, read `check$messages` and decide whether
the warnings need attention before fitting. When the status is `ready`, or you
have decided to proceed after reviewing warnings, fit the imputation model:

```{r file-input-fit, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(traits, tree, gnn = FALSE)
completed <- completed_data(result)
pigauto_report(result)
```

The report gives a compact view of the fitted workflow and its diagnostics.
Read it alongside `completed`; it does not replace checking the values or
assessing prediction accuracy against held-back measurements.

`check_pigauto()` and `completed_data()` were added in 0.11.0. If your
installed version is 0.10.0, call `impute(traits, tree)` directly; that
version does not have them.

`check_pigauto()` is fit-free. Read its printed result before fitting; it
reports readiness and any warnings or input problems. Its default `gnn = FALSE`
matches `impute()` and does not probe torch; pass `gnn = TRUE` when planning a
GNN fit to include runtime availability. Resolve structured input errors before fitting, and
inspect `check$species$matched`, `check$species$data_only`, and
`check$species$tree_only` when labels do not reconcile. `completed` preserves observed values and contains fills only
for modeled missing cells. `result$prediction` is an all-cell diagnostic
output; its uncertainty is type-dependent, and conformal bounds are nominal
held-out diagnostics. A `pigauto_result` by itself does not establish that
downstream inference is reliable. For continuous-only data with one row per
species and no user covariates,
`multi_impute(draws_method = "posterior")` provides the documented posterior
route. For one incomplete continuous covariate in a specified regression,
`multi_impute_analysis()` provides a separate experimental route. Read the
[multiple-imputation guide](multiple-imputation.html) for eligibility,
assumptions, and the current validation limits of both routes.

`read_traits()` requires unique species identifiers. For repeated observations,
use `read.csv()` and supply `species_col = "species"` to both the check and
`impute()`.

### Common declarations for your own data

These are separate templates, not additional steps in the bundled bird
example. Choose only the pattern that matches your data, and replace the
example column names with columns in your own trait table. Each example assumes
that `traits` and `tree` are already loaded.

**Ordered categories**

```{r declaration-ordinal, eval=FALSE}
traits$threat <- ordered(
  traits$threat,
  levels = c(
    "LC", "NT", "VU", "EN", "CR"
  )
)
result <- impute(traits, tree)
```

**An integer-valued measurement treated as continuous**

```{r declaration-integer-continuous, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(
  traits, tree,
  trait_types = c(
    length_mm = "continuous"
  )
)
```

**Proportions and zero-inflated counts**

Numeric proportions and zero-inflated counts need explicit type declarations.

```{r declaration-proportion-zi-count, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(
  traits, tree,
  trait_types = c(
    cover = "proportion",
    parasites = "zi_count"
  )
)
```

**Compositional data**

These grouped columns must be observed or missing together by row and sum to
one when observed.

```{r declaration-composition, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(
  traits, tree,
  multi_proportion_groups = list(
    diet = c(
      "diet_insect",
      "diet_fruit",
      "diet_seed"
    )
  )
)
```

## What pigauto does

Many comparative datasets have missing trait values: species were not
measured, specimens were unavailable, or data were lost. pigauto fills
in those gaps using three sources of information:

1. **The phylogenetic tree.** Closely related species tend to share
   similar traits, so known values of relatives are informative about
   missing ones.
2. **Cross-trait correlations.** If body mass predicts beak length,
   then observed masses help impute missing beak lengths even when the
   species itself was never measured for that trait.
3. **Environmental covariates** (optional). Climate, habitat, or
   geographic variables can improve imputation when trait variation
   has a strong environmental component beyond phylogenetic signal.

The package handles continuous measurements, counts, binary variables,
ordered categories, unordered categories, bounded proportions,
zero-inflated counts, and compositional multi-proportion data — all in a
single call to `impute()`.

### How it works (briefly)

By default pigauto fits a phylogenetic baseline: Brownian-motion
conditional imputation for continuous-family latent columns and
phylogenetic label propagation or a threshold model for discrete traits,
with a per-trait Pagel's lambda. The architecture article explains how
pigauto selects among these baselines. A held-out
validation split calibrates the blend and the conformal intervals.
Split conformal assumes the calibration cells resemble the scored
cells. Masking a whole clade can violate that assumption: residuals from
other clades may not represent the held-out clade, so nominal coverage
need not hold there.
For the current implementation, treat these intervals as nominal diagnostics,
not a general 95% coverage guarantee: validation data also inform model
selection and gate calibration. See the [interval limitations](gnn-architecture.html#uncertainty-quantification).

An optional graph neural network (GNN) is trained when you set `gnn = TRUE`.
It can learn additional patterns from tree topology, cross-trait structure,
and user `covariates`. Covariates can also enter a covariate-aware per-column
numeric baseline when that fallback is selected. Joint MVN and threshold-joint
routes omit them and emit a separate baseline warning. One-versus-rest
categorical routes also omit covariates but do not trigger that warning
themselves. In a mixed fit, another selected joint route can still trigger it. Validation selects how much the GNN contributes
for each trait. The default is `gnn = FALSE`. In the tested
single-observation benchmarks, adding the GNN did not improve held-out
prediction and took longer to fit. A later repeated-observation study with
covariates found gains over the same fitted model without its neural
contribution in two prespecified scenarios, but not in a no-signal control;
separately fitted GLS had lower error in the interactive scenario. These are
different settings and comparisons, not evidence of general GNN superiority.
See the [validation results and their limits](validation-results.html#when-does-the-neural-component-add-predictive-value)
for details. For the implementation name and code map, see the optional
[architecture article](gnn-architecture.html#where-to-look-in-the-code).

The phylogenetic structure is encoded as:

- A symmetric-normalised Gaussian-kernel adjacency matrix derived from
  cophenetic (patristic) distances.
- *k* Laplacian eigenvectors as node positional features — these encode
  phylogenetic clusters at multiple scales.

```{r load}
library(pigauto)
library(ape)
```

## Optional technical walkthrough

The sections below trace each stage for readers who want more control than the
single-call example in **Start here**. You can use that example without
following this walkthrough.

### How the imputation pipeline works

The workflow above is the primary interface. The following is the
fine-grained pipeline for inspection, caching, or benchmarking.

This template assumes you already have a trait data frame named `traits` and
a matching phylogenetic tree named `tree`. If you are following the bundled
bird example, run the AVONET setup in the next section first and use
`avonet300` and `tree300` in place of those placeholders.

```{r quickstart, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(traits, tree)

result$completed    # observed values preserved; some missing values may remain NA
result$imputed_mask # TRUE marks missing targets in fitted rows, not successful fills
result$prediction$se # per-cell, type-dependent uncertainty summaries
```

`impute()` runs the full pipeline internally: preprocessing, baseline fitting,
graph construction, calibration, and prediction (plus GNN training when
`gnn = TRUE`). The rest of this
vignette walks through each step individually for users who need fine-grained
control, want to cache intermediate objects, or are benchmarking components.

### The AVONET bird data

pigauto ships with `avonet300`, a 300-species subset of the AVONET v3 bird
morphology database (Tobias et al. 2022, *Ecology Letters*), and `tree300`.
The bundled tree is member 69 of the 100-tree BirdTree collection, from the
Hackett-backbone set, and pruned to those 300 species; see `?tree300` for the
package-specific extraction record. Hackett et al. (2008) describes the
backbone. The tree is an example, not an MCC or
consensus tree or a recommendation for substantive analyses. For your own
analysis, obtain a tree suited to your taxa and cite Jetz et al. (2012) for
the BirdTree distribution. If you use the BirdTree website, also cite
BirdTree.org. You can download a tree file and
read it with `read_tree()`; see [BirdTree downloads](https://birdtree.org/downloads/)
and the [tree-uncertainty article](tree-uncertainty.html) for options.

```{r data}
data(avonet300, tree300, package = "pigauto")

head(avonet300)
ape::Ntip(tree300)
```

The four morphological columns are example measurements. The dataset also
includes two categorical traits and one ordinal trait, so this walk-through
uses seven original traits in total. Their distributions and phylogenetic
signal vary; this tutorial does not use them to establish a general performance
claim.

### Step 1: Preprocess

`preprocess_traits()` log-transforms and z-scores the traits, and reorders
rows to match the phylogeny's tip order (required by the graph operations).

```{r preprocess}
traits <- avonet300[, -1]              # drop Species_Key column
rownames(traits) <- avonet300$Species_Key

pd <- preprocess_traits(traits, tree300, log_transform = TRUE)
print(pd)
```

The object `pd` is a `pigauto_data` list containing:

- `X_scaled`: the z-scored, log-transformed latent matrix (300 × 14). The four
  continuous traits and the ordinal trait each use one latent column; the two
  categorical traits expand to one column per level.
- `means`, `sds`: per-trait normalisation parameters (for back-transformation)
- `log_transform`: `TRUE`, recorded so `predict()` can invert it automatically

`log_transform = TRUE` (the default) logs every continuous trait whose observed
values are all positive. If a trait is already on a log scale, such as log body
mass, set `log_transform = FALSE` (and log any raw traits yourself), or it will be
imputed on a log(log) scale; see `?impute`.

### Step 2: Create evaluation splits

We hold out 25% of eligible observed species-by-trait entries for evaluation.
All latent columns that encode a selected trait are held out together. These
values are *not* used during training or baseline fitting; they let you assess
prediction error under this masking design. The scores may differ when
real-world missingness follows another pattern.

```{r splits}
splits <- make_missing_splits(pd$X_scaled, missing_frac = 0.25, seed = 42,
                              trait_map = pd$trait_map)

cat("Held-out latent cells:", length(splits$val_idx) + length(splits$test_idx), "\n")
cat("  Validation:", length(splits$val_idx), "\n")
cat("  Test:      ", length(splits$test_idx), "\n")
```

The missing cells are split further: validation cells guide model selection,
while test cells assess predictions under this masking design. Test scores can
differ from performance on naturally missing values if the masking design does
not resemble the real pattern of missingness.

### Step 3: Fit the BM baseline

`fit_baseline()` fits the phylogenetic BM baseline after masking the held-out cells. This
gives the benchmark against which an optional GNN would be compared.

```{r baseline, eval=TRUE}
baseline <- fit_baseline(pd, tree300, splits = splits, model = "BM")

cat("Baseline object contains:\n")
cat("  mu matrix:", nrow(baseline$mu), "x", ncol(baseline$mu), "\n")
cat("  se matrix:", nrow(baseline$se), "x", ncol(baseline$se), "\n")
```

### Step 4: Build the phylogenetic graph

`build_phylo_graph()` computes the adjacency matrix and Laplacian spectral
features from the tree. The result can be cached to disk for reuse.

```{r graph, eval=TRUE}
graph <- build_phylo_graph(
  tree300,
  k_eigen    = 8,
  sigma_mult = 0.5
)

cat("Graph: n =", graph$n, "species\n")
cat("Adjacency: [", nrow(graph$adj), "x", ncol(graph$adj), "]\n")
cat("Spectral coords: [", nrow(graph$coords), "x", ncol(graph$coords), "]\n")
cat("Kernel bandwidth sigma:", round(graph$sigma, 3), "\n")
```

For repeated runs, supply `cache_path = "graph_cache.rds"` to skip
recomputation.

### Step 5: Train the model

With the default `gnn = FALSE`, `fit_pigauto()` fits no network and makes
no torch calls; it calibrates the baseline and the conformal intervals.
The chunk below sets `gnn = TRUE` to show the optional GNN. Its training loop corrupts a random 55% of observed cells each epoch with a
learnable mask token, then minimises a type-appropriate loss on those
known values. A shrinkage penalty keeps GNN predictions closer to the
phylogenetic baseline. For typed data, early stopping monitors a composite held-out validation
loss: each trait contributes a loss suited to its type. Lower is better.
This value is not an RMSE in the original trait units.

```{r train, eval=FALSE}
fit <- fit_pigauto(
  data            = pd,
  tree            = tree300,
  splits          = splits,
  graph           = graph,
  baseline        = baseline,
  hidden_dim      = 64,
  k_eigen         = 8,
  dropout         = 0.10,
  lr              = 3e-3,
  epochs          = 2000,
  corruption_rate = 0.55,
  lambda_shrink   = 0.03,
  eval_every      = 100,
  patience        = 10,
  verbose         = TRUE,
  seed            = 1,
  gnn             = TRUE
)
```

With `verbose = TRUE`, each evaluation reports training-loss components
(`rec`, `shrink`, and `gate`), the learning rate, and, when validation
data are available, the current and best validation loss and remaining
patience.
The exact values depend on your data and settings. For this mixed-type
example, `val` is a composite loss, not an RMSE in Mass units.

```{r print-fit, eval=FALSE}
print(fit)
```

The fit contains seven original traits and 14 latent columns. Its summary
reports the original trait names and the mix of continuous, categorical, and
ordinal types. Do not interpret the latent-column count as the number of input
traits.

### Step 6: Predict

`predict.pigauto_fit()` returns predictions on the original (non-log) scale.
If you request `n_imputations > 1`, it also returns stochastic
prediction-diagnostic draws. These draws are not validated multiple
imputations for downstream inference. For that question, first check whether
your analysis meets a supported route in the
[multiple-imputation guide](multiple-imputation.html).

```{r predict, eval=FALSE}
pred <- predict(fit, return_se = TRUE)

# pred$imputed: 300-row data.frame with the 7 original trait columns
# pred$imputed_latent: 300 x 14 matrix on the latent scale
# pred$se: 300 x 7 per-trait uncertainty matrix
head(pred$imputed)

# Conformal prediction intervals (nominal held-out diagnostic)
pred$conformal_lower[, "Mass"]    # lower bound per species (original units)
pred$conformal_upper[, "Mass"]    # upper bound per species (original units)
# Coverage is not stored on the prediction object. Score it with evaluate()
# (or evaluate_imputation() on held-out cells).
```

The categorical columns in `pred$imputed` are returned as factors. For those
traits, `pred$se` contains uncertainty scores rather than Gaussian standard
errors. The latent prediction has one column per encoded category, while the
decoded data frame has one column per original trait.

### Step 7: Evaluate — and read the gate

`evaluate_imputation()` scores held-out cells on the scale that matches
the trait type. For a single latent column in this mixed-trait fit, no direct covariates
are supplied and the mean safety floor is off. On **high-signal
morphometrics** (AVONET-like mass, beak, tarsus, wing), the calibrated neural
weight for a latent column can be zero (`fit$r_cal_gnn = 0`), leaving the
phylogenetic baseline in this example. In other routes, a zero neural weight closes only the GNN component;
inspect the BM, GNN, and mean weights and any direct covariate terms to
understand the full prediction.

```{r evaluate, eval=FALSE}
# Held-out scores (z-score RMSE for continuous traits)
# Mask validation/test cells before scoring; plain predict() is for imputation.
pred_eval <- predict(fit, evaluation = TRUE)
evaluate_imputation(pred_eval, pd$X_scaled, splits)

# Per-trait calibrated gate. 0 means baseline-only.
fit$r_cal
```

Do not treat a GNN-versus-BM table as the default story. If the gate is
closed, a lower GNN training loss on masked cells is not a claim that
the ensemble beat BM on the test cells you ship. How much (if anything)
the GNN adds depends on the trait, clade, missingness pattern, and
whether calibration left the gate open.

### Step 8: Visualise

#### Training history

```{r plot-history, eval=FALSE}
plot(fit, type = "history")
```

This plot shows the validation loss used for early stopping. For this
mixed-type fit, it is a composite loss, not RMSE in the original trait
units.

#### Uncertainty ribbons

```{r plot-uncertainty, eval=FALSE}
plot(pred, type = "intervals", trait = "Mass")
```

Species are sorted by predicted mass. The blue ribbon shows the conformal
prediction interval when conformal scores are available. Grey points (if
`truth` is supplied) show known values — a useful visual check of calibration.

## Further workflows

Use these sections after completing the basic or technical walkthrough.

### Experimental analysis-aware multiple imputation

Downstream inference requires imputations compatible with the substantive
analysis. `multi_impute_analysis()` therefore receives the formula and model
class before drawing one incomplete continuous covariate under MAR.

This interface implements a narrow, experimental workflow. In the
registered analysis-aware tests, 23 of 24 method-by-scenario results were
indeterminate and one binomial-logit GLM result failed; none was classified
as supported. These 24 results include 12 complete-data controls. See the
[registered inferential results](validation-results.html#inferential-results).

This is a template, not a standalone example: `analysis_data` must contain a
continuous outcome `y`, one incomplete continuous predictor `x`, and a fully
observed continuous predictor `z`. This example selects the Gaussian `lm`
route; change both the outcome and model setting if your analysis uses another
supported outcome type.

```{r mi-workflow, eval=FALSE}
analysis_data$z_sq <- analysis_data$z^2

mi <- multi_impute_analysis(
  data = analysis_data,
  formula = y ~ x + z,
  missing = "x",
  model = "lm",
  m = 50L,
  auxiliary = "z_sq",
  seed = 1L
)

fits <- with_imputations(mi, function(d) lm(y ~ x + z, data = d))
pool_mi(fits)
```

The initial dispatch is deliberately narrow: proper Bayesian normal-regression
MI for Gaussian `lm`, `smcfcs` for binomial-logit `glm`, and `jomo.smc` for a
Gaussian `lmer` with one random intercept. Users must precompute auxiliary
terms such as `z_sq`. Fixed effects are the only supported pooling targets.

Conformal-width, Brownian/MC-dropout, and PMM draws remain experimental
prediction diagnostics. They failed the downstream fixed-effect gate and must
not be passed to `with_imputations()`/`pool_mi()` for inference. For continuous traits with one row per species and no covariates,
`multi_impute()` with its default `draws_method = "auto"` selects posterior
draws when the data meet its eligibility conditions. This is a software
capability. The documented downstream route fits analyses linear in the
imputed continuous traits on their imputation scale and uses variables
among those traits; it does not establish calibrated inference. In the
registered validation, five of eight posterior slope regimes failed and
three were indeterminate; no inferential scenario was classified as
supported. See the
[registered inferential results](validation-results.html#inferential-results)
and [multiple imputation article](multiple-imputation.html) for scope and
conditions.


### Phylogenetic tree uncertainty

Use `multi_impute_trees()` to see whether point predictions change across a
posterior sample of trees. This is a prediction-sensitivity check only; its
outputs do not provide inferential uncertainty for downstream estimates and
cannot be pooled for inference. See the
[tree-sensitivity guide](tree-uncertainty.html) for a step-by-step example.

### Active imputation: where to measure next

`suggest_next_observation()` returns model-based BM/label-propagation proxy
rankings under its stated assumptions. It is not an optimal sampling guarantee
or a demonstrated field gain.

```{r active-impute, eval=FALSE}
res <- impute(traits, tree300)

# Top-10 individual (species, trait) cells, ordered by expected
# total variance reduction:
suggest_next_observation(res, top_n = 10, by = "cell")

# Or aggregated by species (sum of variance reductions across the
# species' currently-missing continuous-family traits):
suggest_next_observation(res, top_n = 10, by = "species")
```

The `delta_var_total` column is the model-based expected reduction
in total predictive variance across all currently-missing cells if
you observed that candidate next:

\[
\Delta V(s_{\text{new}}) = \sigma_t^2 \sum_{i \in \mathrm{miss}_t}
\frac{D_{ik}^2}{\alpha_k}
\]

where \(D = R_{mm} - R_{mo} R_{oo}^{-1} R_{om}\) is the residual
matrix at currently-missing cells, \(\alpha_k = D_{kk}\) is the
current relative leverage of cell \(k\), and \(\sigma_t^2\) is
the REML BM variance. Treat it as a proxy ranking conditional on the fitted
model, rather than a claim about a future sampling campaign.

**Scope.** `suggest_next_observation()` v2 (2026-05-01) supports
all eight pigauto trait types:

* **Variance reduction** for continuous-family traits (`continuous`,
  `count`, `ordinal`, `proportion`) and the magnitude column of
  `zi_count`, computed by closed-form Sherman-Morrison rank-1
  update on the BM phylogenetic-correlation matrix.
* **Entropy reduction** for `binary`, `categorical`, and the gate
  column of `zi_count`, computed by closed-form label-propagation
  posteriors.
* **Multi-component variance reduction** (per-component BM,
  summed across the K CLR-z latent columns) for `multi_proportion`.

For `zi_count` rows the output populates BOTH `delta_var_total`
(probability-weighted magnitude variance reduction) AND
`delta_entropy_total` (gate entropy reduction); the `metric`
column is set to `"variance"` so rows sort on the magnitude scale.
See `?suggest_next_observation` for full details.

**Variance vs entropy are not directly comparable** — ordering across
metrics by `delta_var_total` is approximate. When you
want a strict ranking on a single metric, filter by `metric`
first or restrict `types` to continuous-family-only or
discrete-only.

Multi-obs (multiple observations per species) inputs are not
supported and error with a clear message.

### Advanced controls

These templates assume your own trait table is named `traits` and its
matching phylogeny is named `tree`. In the bundled bird walkthrough above,
use `tree300` in place of `tree`.

#### Solver, calibration, EM, and refinement

```{r advanced-controls, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(
  traits, tree,
  joint_solver = "rphylopars",
  em_iterations = 2L,
  joint_refine_iter = 1L,
  conformal_split_val = TRUE
)
```

#### Exact conditional prediction route

```{r exact-route, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(traits, tree, predict_method = "exact")
```

#### Phylogenetic-signal gating

`impute()` can run a per-trait Pagel's-λ check before training when
`phylo_signal_gate = TRUE`. Traits below the threshold are routed to the
grand-mean corner when `safety_floor = TRUE`, or to the Brownian-baseline
corner when it is `FALSE`. This is a calibration choice, not evidence that
the trait has no predictive structure, and it does not skip model training.
This can protect against
over-fitting noise on traits where the phylogeny carries little
information.

It is **off by default** (`phylo_signal_gate = FALSE`, and likewise
`safety_floor = FALSE`). In the tested settings with Pagel's λ estimated
for every trait type (`discrete_lambda = "estimate"`), the gate did not
improve accuracy; this result is specific to those settings and is not a
general performance claim. To turn it on, use the arguments below:

```{r phylo-signal-gate, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(traits, tree,
                 phylo_signal_gate     = TRUE,   # opt-in (default FALSE)
                 safety_floor          = TRUE,   # enables the grand-mean fallback
                 phylo_signal_threshold = 0.2,   # default; min lambda to keep BM/GNN
                 phylo_signal_method   = "lambda")
```

If a trait's λ falls below `phylo_signal_threshold`, the calibrated
gate routes it to the mean when `safety_floor = TRUE` and to the Brownian
baseline when `safety_floor = FALSE`. `print(fit)` reports
which traits triggered the gate and their λ values.

To disable it explicitly (this is the default):

```{r phylo-signal-gate-off, eval=FALSE}
result <- impute(traits, tree, phylo_signal_gate = FALSE)
```

#### Assembling covariates from public data

Two helpers are bundled for the common case of building a
covariate matrix from species-level environmental data:

```{r covariate-helpers, eval=FALSE}
# Step 1: GBIF occurrence centroids (median lat/lon across cleaned points)
gbif <- pull_gbif_centroids(species          = rownames(my_traits),
                            cache_dir        = "cache/gbif",
                            occurrence_limit = 500L,
                            store_points     = TRUE,
                            refresh_cache    = TRUE)
#> data.frame with columns species, centroid_lat, centroid_lon, n_occurrences

# Step 2: WorldClim bioclim summaries (median + IQR of all 19 bio variables
# across each species' GBIF occurrences)
clim <- pull_worldclim_per_species(species             = rownames(my_traits),
                                    gbif_cache_dir      = "cache/gbif",
                                    worldclim_cache_dir = "cache/worldclim",
                                    resolution          = "10m",
                                    refresh_cache       = TRUE)
#> data.frame with bio1..bio19 medians + IQRs + n_extracted per species

# Check the species order before fitting: covariate rows must match trait rows.
stopifnot(identical(clim$species, rownames(my_traits)))

# Step 3: keep the intended numeric climate summaries, not species or count
climate_cols <- grep("^bio[0-9]+_(median|iqr)$", names(clim), value = TRUE)
clim_cov <- clim[, climate_cols, drop = FALSE]
if (anyNA(clim_cov)) stop("Resolve missing climate values before fitting")
result <- impute(my_traits, my_tree, covariates = clim_cov, gnn = TRUE)
```

The example refreshes both caches so older centroid-only GBIF extracts are not
mistaken for per-occurrence point data. For routine repeated runs, remove
`refresh_cache = TRUE` after refreshing the caches once. Once you supply
cache directories, both helpers reuse stored extracts on subsequent runs.
GBIF requires no API key. WorldClim raster downloads are
~50–500 MB depending on resolution and are cached in
`worldclim_cache_dir`.  Both functions error with a clear message
if the optional dependencies (`rgbif`, `terra`) are not installed.
Both helpers return one row per requested species. The `species` column is an
alignment key, not a model covariate; use only the numeric climate columns as
shown above, and do not reorder them independently:

For argument details, see `?impute`, `?pull_gbif_centroids`, and
`?pull_worldclim_per_species`.

## Tips and next steps

**Optional GNN: use a GPU if available.** When you set `gnn = TRUE`, pigauto
selects CUDA when available, then Apple MPS, and otherwise CPU. The default
`gnn = FALSE` fits the phylogenetic baseline only and does not call torch. To
check runtime availability before opting into GNN training:

```{r gpu, eval=FALSE}
torch::cuda_is_available()       # NVIDIA GPU
torch::backends_mps_is_available() # Apple Silicon GPU
```

**Cache the phylogenetic graph.** For repeated experiments, save time by
writing the graph to disk:

```{r cache, eval=FALSE}
graph <- build_phylo_graph(tree300, k_eigen = 8, cache_path = "tree300_graph.rds")
```

**Large trees.** `build_phylo_graph()` creates several dense N × N matrices:
cophenetic distances and their squares, adjacency, a Laplacian, and
phylogenetic correlations. A 10,000 × 10,000 matrix stored in double
precision needs about 800 MB for its values alone. Several matrices coexist
while the graph is built, and the squared-distance matrix is retained during
GNN training when enabled, so memory use can be substantial. For trees with
more than 7,500 tips, the spectral step uses the optional `RSpectra` Lanczos
solver when it is installed; if it is unavailable or does not converge, the
function falls back to dense eigendecomposition. `k_eigen = "auto"` limits
the number of returned spectral features to 32, but this does not reduce the
storage needed for the dense matrices. For very large trees or limited
memory, consider pruning to the clade relevant to your analysis.

**Supplying your own data.** The workflow above works for any phylogenetic tree
and trait matrix:

```{r own-data, eval=FALSE}
tree   <- ape::read.tree("my_phylogeny.nwk")
traits <- read_traits("my_traits.csv", species_col = "species")
pd     <- preprocess_traits(traits, tree)
# ...proceed as above
```

Trait columns can be any of eight supported types. Five are
auto-detected from R column class: `numeric` (continuous), `integer`
(count), `factor` with 2 levels (binary), `factor` with >2 levels
(categorical), and `ordered` (ordinal). Three require an explicit
declaration because they cannot be inferred from class alone:
`numeric` (0–1) with a named override such as
`trait_types = c(cover = "proportion")` for bounded proportions; `integer`
with a named override such as `trait_types = c(parasite_load = "zi_count")`
for zero-inflated counts. The override names must match trait-column names.
K `numeric` columns are declared via the
`multi_proportion_groups` argument for compositional (simplex) data
whose rows sum to 1. pigauto reads column classes to decide how each
trait is encoded and imputed. The
species names in `traits` should overlap with tip labels in `tree`. Partial
overlap is allowed: unmatched input species remain in `completed` but are not
modeled or filled. Tree tips with no input row can still be used during model
fitting.

## References

- Tobias, J.A. et al. (2022). AVONET: morphological, ecological and
  geographical data for all birds. *Ecology Letters*, 25, 581–597.
- Jetz, W. et al. (2012). The global diversity of birds in space and time.
  *Nature*, 491, 444–448.
- Hackett, S.J. et al. (2008). A phylogenomic study of birds reveals their
  evolutionary history. *Science*, 320(5884), 1763–1768.
  https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1157704
- Goolsby, E.W., Bruggeman, J. & Ané, C. (2017). Rphylopars: fast
  multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods for missing data and
  within-species variation. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 8, 22–27.
  (This provides broad context for conditional multivariate phylogenetic
  models with missing data. pigauto's Brownian baseline uses its own internal
  conditional-MVN implementation; the default route does not call
  `Rphylopars`.)
- Cohn, D.A., Ghahramani, Z. & Jordan, M.I. (1996). Active learning
  with statistical models. *Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research*,
  4, 129–145. The paper discusses selecting observations to reduce expected
  model variance. This is general active-learning background; it does not
  validate pigauto's phylogenetic variance-reduction calculation or guarantee
  better field sampling.
